beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Onkar Bhujbal. If you work out a hard equation today, you do not solve it again from scratch tomorrow — you remember the answer. Computers, by default, are not that considerate. Unless you tell them otherwise, they will run the same expensive machine learning calculation a thousand times in a row and charge you for every one. Today: caching, latency, and why scaling an A.I. system is mostly a memory problem.

beats.narration_text: A cache does not make anything faster. It makes you stop doing work you already did — which looks identical from the outside, right up until the answer changes underneath you.

beats.narration_text: Computer science has a standing trade between time and space. With large language models and vector databases, time is the expensive side: inference burns accelerator cycles you are billed for, and the user waits while it happens. Memory is the cheap side — not cheap per gigabyte, but absurdly cheap compared to recomputing an embedding. So engineers spend space to buy time, and store the answers to questions that cost real money to ask.

props.stampSub: RAM is not cheap per gigabyte — it is cheap next to inference

beats.honesty_note: The script calls RAM 'cheap and abundant'. Scoped on screen and in the VO: RAM is expensive per gigabyte and strictly limited; it is cheap only relative to recomputing inference. That relative comparison is the whole argument, so it is worth stating precisely.

beats.narration_text: In-memory data stores like Redis and Memcached sit in front of the expensive layer. They keep their working set in R.A.M. rather than reading from disk, which is why a lookup lands in single-digit milliseconds instead of hundreds. One correction to how this usually gets explained: Redis is not inherently volatile — it can write snapshots and an append-only log to disk. What is true is that you should treat a cache as volatile, because anything you cannot rebuild from the source of truth does not belong in one.

beats.honesty_note: CORRECTION to the supplied script, stated in the VO: the script says Redis 'stores data entirely in volatile RAM' and that power loss means the data vanishes. Redis supports RDB snapshots and AOF persistence. The defensible claim is the discipline, not the mechanism — treat a cache as disposable. Latency figures are directional: a local Redis GET is typically sub-millisecond, single-digit ms once a network hop is involved.

beats.narration_text: Now the hard part, and it is famously hard. If the underlying truth changes, the cache does not know. It will keep handing out the old answer with total confidence, and nothing in your logs will look wrong. The standard fix is a time-to-live — the entry deletes itself after an hour. But be precise about what that buys. A one-hour T.T.L. does not prevent stale answers. It caps them at one hour of confidently serving something false.

props.stampSub: a TTL chooses how much staleness you accept — it does not remove it

beats.authoring_note: The script presents TTL as the solution ('ensuring the cache periodically deletes itself'). Sharpened rather than contradicted: TTL is the right tool and it is a staleness BUDGET, not a correctness guarantee. Where staleness is unacceptable, you invalidate on write instead.

beats.act: SCENE 4b — THE BUG A TTL CANNOT REACH (added)
beats.narration_text: And there is a worse failure that no expiry will save you from. A cache is only as correct as its key. If the key leaves out something the answer actually depended on — which document set was searched, which model version answered, which user was asking — then two different questions collapse into one entry, and the second caller gets the first caller's answer. That is not slow. That is wrong, it is instant, and across tenants it is a data leak. Key on everything the answer depends on, or do not cache it.

beats.authoring_note: BEAT ADDED. The script's invalidation scene covers staleness over TIME and prescribes TTL. It does not cover under-specified keys, which is the failure a TTL cannot touch: the entry is fresh and still wrong. The cross-tenant case makes it a confidentiality issue, not only a correctness one.

beats.narration_text: So put a memory layer in front of your expensive compute — and write the key as though someone else's answer depends on getting it right, because it does. Trade space for time. Then go and look at what your key leaves out.

props.title: cache.py

beats.narration_text: Here is the prompt worth running against your own cache. Ask a model what two different requests could produce the same key in your code, and what the second caller would receive. If it finds one, you did not have a performance optimisation — you had a bug that happened to be fast.
